cards.def: The chapter opens with Col. Daniel Jordan and his 261 slaves at Laurel Hill, a Texas cotton man, Sam Williams at Buffalo Forge, runaway Octave Johnson in the Louisiana swamps, and yeoman Ferdinand Steel, who never made enough to buy even one slave.

After "Alabama Fever" drew settlers into the Black Belt, cotton spread to the Red River and Texas in the 1840s, and by the eve of the Civil War nearly a third of the crop came from west of the Mississippi.

cards.term: Example of the domestic slave trade's human cost
cards.def: Upper South slaveholders sold 2 million people to the Deep South, separating one-fifth of husbands and wives there and one-third of all children from their parents, and from 1820 to 1860 such sales separated perhaps 600,000 husbands and wives.

cards.term: Example of how rural the cotton South remained
cards.def: In 1860, 84 percent of the southern labor force still farmed, compared with 40 percent in the North, the South made only 9 percent of the nation's manufactures, and only 1 in 10 southerners lived in cities, compared with 1 out of 3 northerners.

cards.term: Example of the planter elite's narrow base
cards.def: Only about one-quarter of white southerners belonged to slaveowning families, only about 1 in 30 to the planter class, and the richest 1,000 cotton families had about $50 million in income, compared with about $60 million for 666,000 other families.

cards.term: Example of the cotton frontier's boom mentality
cards.def: One description of the cotton kingdom's logic was "To sell cotton in order to buy negroes—to make more cotton to buy more negroes, 'ad infinitum.'"

cards.term: Example of a plantation mistress's complaint
cards.def: Susan Dabney Smedes wrote that "the mistress of a plantation was the most complete slave on it," and Mary Chesnut recorded the miscegenation white wives were expected to ignore.

cards.term: Example of yeoman pride and racial solidarity
cards.def: Olmsted quoted the attitude that ordinary whites "would all think themselves as good as" planters, helping explain why a nonslaveowning majority still defended slavery.

cards.term: Example of the gang system at work
cards.def: In 1854 Olmsted watched Mississippi field hands return after a thunderstorm: 40 of the largest women with hoes led by an old driver carrying a whip, then about 30 plowhands, and a white overseer bringing up the rear.

cards.term: Example of the standard weekly ration
cards.def: Adults typically received about a peck of cornmeal, 3 or 4 pounds of bacon or salt pork, and molasses, almost 5,400 calories but a monotonous diet that lacked essential nutrients and was linked to pellagra and beriberi.

cards.term: Example of rare but terrifying organized revolt
cards.def: In 1831 Nat Turner, a literate slave preacher, and six confederates murdered his master's family, gained some 70 recruits, and killed 57 whites, after which white southerners tightened control and soon closed ranks in slavery's defense.

cards.term: Example of hidden protest in spirituals
cards.def: Frederick Douglass disclosed that slaves who sang longingly of "Canaan, sweet Canaan" were thinking of the North and freedom, and "Steal Away to Jesus" sung in the fields could signal a secret meeting that night.
In the best-known slave folktales, the weak but cunning Brer Rabbit defeated larger animals such as Brer Fox and Brer Bear by using his wits, teaching young slaves how to survive in a hostile world.

cards.term: Example of the Virginia Debate's outcome
cards.def: From January 16 to 25, 1832, the Virginia legislature debated the future of slavery and then refused to act, 73 to 58, the last full-scale consideration of the institution in a southern state before the Civil War.
